plot: Second person, 'Why You Wouldn't Survive' format: you walk the Oregon Trail in 1850; twelve chapters answer daily-life questions (cost of the outfit, the wagon, food and buffalo chips, a typical day, sleep and water, river crossings, cholera, accidents, deadlines and the Donner party, the things you throw out, graves dug in the road), and the last chapter is the true grave of Rebecca Winters (died of cholera August 15, 1852), marked by an iron wagon rim, found by railroad surveyors in 1899 and moved in the 1990s.

beats.say: 1850. Two thousand miles of wagon road. About one in ten people who started it never finished.
Wagons roll! Anyone not hitched by seven gets left behind!
Wait for me! I only just found my shoes!
This is the Oregon Trail. You are about to walk it.
Why would you not survive it? Let's go through your life, one question at a time.
Food. Sleep. Water. Rivers. And the one thing that killed more people than anything else.
And at the very end, a grave that nobody can explain.
Chapter one. Why would anyone leave?
Between 1840 and 1860, somewhere around four hundred thousand people made this trip.
Free land. That's the promise. In Oregon, a married couple could claim six hundred and forty acres.
That's about five hundred football fields. For free.
But first, you have to buy your outfit. That means the wagon, the animals and a year of supplies.
In 1850, that cost about eight hundred to twelve hundred dollars.
For many workers back then, that was more than a whole year of pay.
So you sell the farm. You sell the furniture. And you start walking.
Mom isn't sure about this. Neither are the oxen.
We sold the house for a trail of dust. I hope you're right.
Chapter two. Your wagon.
In the movies, they ride in it. In real life, almost nobody does.
The wagon has no springs. Every rock on the road goes straight through your spine.
It's a little longer than the bed of a pickup truck. And about four feet wide.
Everything you own has to fit in there. Food, tools, clothes, and the kids' toys.
Oxen pull it. Oxen are slow, but they're tough. They can eat the prairie grass and keep going.
So you walk. Beside the wagon, for the whole way. Even the kids.
Two thousand miles. In these shoes. This is fine.
Chapter three. What do you eat?
Guidebooks told each adult to pack about two hundred pounds of flour.
Add about seventy-five pounds of bacon, plus beans, rice, dried fruit, sugar, and coffee.
That's not a lot of variety. You'll eat bread, bacon and beans, again and again.
If you're lucky, a hunter shoots a buffalo. If you're not, you cook what you can find.
In desperate times, people ate prairie dogs. And snakes.
And what do you burn for your fire? There are almost no trees on the plains.
You burn dried buffalo droppings. They called them buffalo chips.
Don't make that face. You'll be cooking with them too.
The good news is, the grass was free. The bad news is, so was the dust.
Chapter four. A day on the trail.
Four in the morning. The wagon leader fires a rifle. Time to get up.
By five, breakfast is cooking. The men and boys round up the animals.
At seven, the wagon master yells it. Wagons roll!
And then you walk. About twelve to fifteen miles, every single day.
Fifteen miles is about two hundred and twenty football fields. And you do it again tomorrow.
You stop for an hour at noon. They called it nooning. Then you walk some more.
Kids have daily chores too. One of them is collecting buffalo chips. Hold your nose.
Dust gets in your teeth, your eyes, your bread, and your hair. It never leaves.
Around six, the wagons form a circle. That's not for fighting. It's a pen for the animals.
Some nights, someone pulls out a fiddle. People sing and dance in the dust. It's the best part of the day.
Then you cook, you eat, you fall asleep. And at four, the rifle fires again.
A trip like this took four to six months. Think about that. Half a year of walking.
Chapter five. Where do you sleep? And where do you drink?
You sleep in a tent, or under the wagon, or on the ground. No bed. No door.
Prairie storms hit fast. Hail. Lightning. Wind that rips a tent right off the ground.
And the water? Camps were picked by where water and grass were.
Sometimes the water is clean. Sometimes it's a muddy pond where a hundred oxen just drank.
In dry summers, the water holes dried up. The animals died. Families went thirsty.
And a bathroom? There isn't one. The whole prairie is the bathroom, and you hope for a bush.
Your wagon cover is canvas coated with oil. It blocks some rain. Not all of it. And it flaps all night long.
Is it safe to drink this? Anyone? Hello?
Remember that question. It matters later.
Chapter six. The rivers.
The trail crosses the Platte, the Snake, the Green, and dozens more.
There are no bridges. You float the wagon across, or you pay a ferry.
Three dollars a wagon. Cash. No swimming for free.
Three dollars in 1850 was a lot, so many families tried to cross on their own.
They took off the wheels. They sealed the wagon box with tar. And they floated it.
A strong current can flip a wagon like a toy. And people don't swim in wool clothes.
Drowning was one of the main killers on the trail.
And the rivers were the part that people wrote home about.
Chapter seven. The thing that really kills you.
People feared attacks. They feared snakes. They feared starving.
But the number one killer, by a wide margin, was disease.
And the worst of all was cholera.
Cholera comes from dirty water. Remember that muddy pond?
It hit hardest in the years when the most wagons went west, like 1849 and 1852.
A hundred wagon trains used the same river bank. The same camps. The same water.
You'd feel fine at breakfast. A slight fever in the morning.
By noon, you can't stand up. By evening, you could be gone.
People often died within twelve hours of the first symptoms.
Doctors back then had camphor and laudanum. Those only dulled the pain.
Over the years, up to thirty thousand people may have died from disease on the trail.
The Park Service says that works out to ten to fifteen deaths for every mile.
Every mile. For two thousand miles.
Keep walking. We can't stop. Stopping is worse.
Chapter eight. Accidents.
After disease, accidents were the second biggest killer.
Children fell off wagons and under the wheels. A wagon can weigh a ton or more.
Guns went off by accident. Everyone carried one, and nobody had safety training.
Oxen stampeded. Wagons rolled down steep hills. Ropes snapped.
In fact, a long, steep hill meant tying a rope to the back of the wagon. And hoping.
The trail was a hundred small ways to die. Every day. For months.
What about the attacks you heard about?
Historians say Native Americans killed about four hundred emigrants before 1860.
Compare that to thousands from cholera. The movies got that part backward.
Chapter nine. The deadlines.
You can't take your time. There's a clock, and it's the weather.
Leave in mid-April or May, when the grass is green enough for your animals.
Reach Fort Kearny, in Nebraska, by about May fifteenth.
Reach Fort Laramie, in Wyoming, by mid June.
And be at South Pass, in the mountains, by the Fourth of July.
On the way, you pass a huge rock in Wyoming. Travelers carved their names into it. People called it the Register of the Desert.
If you're late, the mountain snow comes before you get through.
The Donner party learned that in 1846. They got stuck in deep snow in the Sierra Nevada.
Many of them did not make it out. You do not want to be late.
Chapter ten. What you leave behind.
Your oxen are tired. The hills get steeper. The wagon is too heavy.
So you start throwing things out. First the extra tools. Then the heavy stove.
Then the trunk of your grandmother's dishes. Then the rocking chair.
My mother carried that chair across an ocean. I can't leave it.
Mom. The oxen can't pull it. We have to.
The trail itself was littered with abandoned furniture. Stoves. Chests. Barrels. Pianos.
The people ahead of you left a trail of everything they loved.
Chapter eleven. When someone dies.
You can't stop the whole train for a funeral. Not for long. The deadline won't wait.
So you dig the grave fast. Often, you dig it right in the trail.
Why? Because then the whole wagon train drives over the dirt.
It packs the ground down. Wolves can't smell where the body is.
So most graves had no marker at all. That was on purpose.
The Park Service calls the trail the nation's longest graveyard.
Estimates say there were at least twenty thousand graves. Almost none are marked.
Chapter twelve. The last grave.
August fifteenth, 1852. A Mormon wagon train is crossing Nebraska. Cholera is in camp.
A woman named Rebecca Winters helps care for the sick. Then she gets sick too.
She dies that same day. She was about fifty years old.
Her family is heading for the Salt Lake Valley, to build a new home there.
Her husband Hiram and a friend named William Reynolds go to bury her.
They do something different. They do not bury her in the road.
They dig a very deep grave away from the trail. They line it with wooden planks.
They wrap her in blankets. They cover her with more planks. They can't stand the thought of dirt touching her.
Then William finds an iron wheel rim from a wagon. At night, by candlelight, he chisels her name into it.
Rebecca Winters, age fifty. The rim is bent into an oval, and it's pushed into the ground.
Then the wagon train rolls on. They have to. They have a deadline.
Her family kept walking. They reached the Salt Lake Valley that October.
For years, her marker is one of the only ones along the whole trail.
Travelers stop there. They look at the iron rim. They think about what's ahead.
Then the railroad comes in 1869. The trail empties out. And Rebecca is forgotten.
In 1899, railroad surveyors are walking the land in Nebraska.
And they find an iron wheel rim in the grass. It's still standing. It still has her name on it.
Forty-seven years of prairie fires, blizzards and storms. And that rim never fell.
The planned railroad line would have gone straight over her grave.
A local landowner fought hard to protect it. The railroad ended up laying track just a few feet away.
Whether the railroad truly changed its route is still debated. The tracks were still only about six feet from the grave.
In the 1990s, the railroad moved her grave. About nine hundred feet east, to a quiet park.
They kept the original iron rim. You can still see it today, in Nebraska.
Out of twenty thousand graves, this is one of the very few you can still find.
Why this one? Because two people refused to bury her the way everyone else did.
So, would you have survived the Oregon Trail?
Most people who went made it. But about one in ten did not.
And they weren't killed by outlaws. They were killed by water, by accidents, and by time.
The lesson is simple. Nobody on that trail was braver than the people who stopped to say a name.
Would you have kept walking? Or would you have stopped? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more true history.

long.title: Why You Wouldn't Survive the Oregon Trail, 1850 🐂
long.description:
Would you have kept walking, or stopped? Tell me in the comments.

Your food, your wagon, your water, the river crossings, and the sickness that killed more people than anything else: what the Oregon Trail was really like in 1850. About one in ten emigrants never finished the 2,000-mile walk. Then the strange last chapter: out of some 20,000 trail graves, one is still marked by an iron wagon rim, and it was almost lost under a railroad.

es.description:

Tu comida, tu carreta, el agua, los ríos y la enfermedad que mató a más gente: cómo era realmente el Camino de Oregón en 1850. Uno de cada diez emigrantes no terminó la caminata de 2.000 millas... y al final, una tumba que sigue marcada con un aro de hierro.

fr.title: Pourquoi vous ne survivriez pas à la piste de l'Oregon en 1850 🐂
fr.description:
Auriez-vous continué à marcher, ou vous seriez-vous arrêté ? Dites-le-moi en commentaire.

Votre nourriture, votre chariot, l'eau, les rivières et la maladie qui a tué le plus de monde : la vraie vie sur la piste de l'Oregon en 1850. Un émigrant sur dix n'est jamais arrivé. Et à la fin, une tombe encore marquée par un cercle de fer.

ja.title: 1850年のオレゴン街道で、あなたが生き残れない理由 🐂
ja.description:
あなたなら歩き続けましたか？それとも立ち止まりましたか？コメントで教えてください。

de.title: Warum du den Oregon Trail 1850 nicht überlebt hättest 🐂
de.description:
